summary: C9 horizon notes. Self-Building AI, acquisition engine, international expansion, IPO infrastructure, edge deployment, Corner for Government v2, the talent marketplace, Corner Capital, and the self-replicating system. The layer where Corner stops needing humans to grow.
content:
CORNER C9 Notes: The Autonomous Company

Author: Steve (AI Advisory Lead) Date: 2026-03-16 Depends on: C8 complete (Corner OS, Hardware, Franchise Model, AI-Native CRM, Government, Open-Source Core, Physical Spaces, Financial Infrastructure, Agent Consciousness, Corner Network) Status: Horizon notes. Pure vision. These become real when C8 is halfway done. The timelines here are 4-5 years out. The landscape will be unrecognizable by then. But the direction is clear.

What C8 Delivered

C8 made Corner the operating system. Files, communication, finance, HR, legal, all running through Corner. Dedicated hardware on desks. Franchise operators in 50+ cities. AI-native CRM replacing Salesforce. FedRAMP opening government. Open-source engine building developer community. Physical coworking spaces proving the concept in the real world. Financial infrastructure processing money. Agent consciousness remembering everything. The Corner Network connecting businesses to each other through their agents.

C8 answered: "How does this become the way people run a business?" By replacing every other tool, one by one, until Corner is the only thing left.

C9 answers: "How does this run itself?"

The C9 Thesis

C1-C4 built a product someone uses. C5 made them stay. C6 let others build and sell it. C7 made it smart. C8 made it the operating system. Every chapter required more humans: more engineers, more sales people, more franchise operators, more customer success reps. C9 reverses that curve.

C9 is where Corner's own AI systems handle the functions that previously required AOM employees. Not replacing people for cruelty or cost-cutting. Replacing bottlenecks so the system can grow at the speed of demand, not the speed of hiring.

The shift: C8 Corner runs the client's business. C9 Corner runs AOM's business.

Patrik and Ash built a system that manages operations for small businesses. C9 is that same system managing the company that builds it. The snake eats its tail. The system operates itself.

1. Self-Building AI (Corner Genesis)

Concept

A client describes their business in natural language. Corner builds the entire agent roster, skills, workflows, room layout, and onboarding context automatically. No human setup. No AOM engineer configures anything. The AI builds the AI.

Why This Is the Real Product

Today (C4), AOM onboards a client in ~2 hours of human time: understanding the business, configuring agents, writing context files, loading skills, testing. At $3,000/month revenue, that 2-hour setup amortizes quickly. But at 10,000 clients, 2 hours each is 20,000 hours of human labor per year. That doesn't scale.

Corner Genesis eliminates setup entirely. The client talks to a Genesis Agent during onboarding. The Genesis Agent asks questions (like the audit questionnaire from the AI advisory product, but evolved). Based on answers, it:

  1. Selects agent types from the full roster (Operations, Calendar, Email, Outreach, Content, Finance, Legal, HR, etc.)
  2. Generates custom system prompts for each agent, tuned to the client's industry, size, and communication style
  3. Installs relevant skills from the marketplace based on the client's industry and stated needs
  4. Builds the initial context files (business description, client roster, priorities, goals)
  5. Configures the room layout (industry-appropriate theme from C7 editions)
  6. Sets up integrations (QuickBooks, Gmail, calendar) via guided OAuth flows
  7. Runs a 5-minute "first day" simulation where the agents demonstrate their capabilities with the client's real data
  8. Hands the client a fully operational Corner office

The Genesis Agent

The Genesis Agent is unlike any other agent in Corner. It doesn't do ongoing work. It builds the system, then steps aside. Think of it as the contractor who builds the house and hands over the keys.

Capabilities:

  • Understands 50+ industry templates (from C7 industry editions, expanded)
  • Knows every agent type's strengths and use cases
  • Can write custom system prompts that capture a business's specific voice, processes, and preferences
  • Generates context files from a conversation (no forms, no uploads, just talking)
  • Tests the configured system by running sample tasks and verifying agent outputs
  • Flags edge cases for human review (unusual industries, conflicting requirements, compliance-sensitive businesses)

Quality gate:

  • Genesis runs a self-QA pass after configuration. Every agent receives a test prompt. If any agent's response quality falls below threshold, Genesis adjusts the configuration.
  • First-week monitoring: Genesis Agent stays dormant but watches. If the client hits friction (repeated questions to agents that get poor responses, tasks that stall), Genesis suggests adjustments: "I noticed your Calendar agent isn't handling your recurring client meetings well. I've updated its context to better understand your scheduling patterns."
  • Human fallback: if Genesis confidence is below 80% on any configuration decision, it flags for AOM review. At C9 maturity, this happens on <5% of signups.

Scale Implications

Without Genesis: AOM can onboard ~20 clients/week (with 2 ops people). With Genesis: AOM can onboard 20 clients/hour. The constraint shifts from labor to infrastructure.

Build Estimate

8-12 weeks for the core Genesis Agent. Ongoing refinement as more industries and edge cases are encountered. The Genesis Agent gets better with every client it configures (its own form of agent consciousness from C8).

2. Acquisition Engine

Concept

AOM acquires small vertical SaaS companies. Migrates their clients to Corner. Instant distribution. Instead of selling Corner to 10,000 businesses one at a time, buy a company with 10,000 businesses already paying for a worse product.

Why Acquisition

Organic growth has a ceiling. Even with Genesis (Feature #1) reducing setup friction to zero, AOM still needs clients to find Corner, evaluate it, and decide to switch. That decision cycle is 30-90 days for most SMBs. Acquisition bypasses the decision entirely: the client's tool becomes Corner overnight.

Target Profile

Ideal acquisition targets:

  • Vertical SaaS for a specific industry (construction, CPA, law, healthcare, restaurants)
  • 500-5,000 paying clients
  • $1-10M ARR
  • Product is good enough that clients stay but not so good that switching to Corner is a downgrade
  • Founder is tired or ready to exit
  • Technology stack is modern enough that data migration is feasible (not a legacy COBOL system)
  • Client base overlaps with Corner's target demographic (SMBs, 5-50 employees, US-based)

Example targets (hypothetical):

  • A scheduling app for contractors with 3,000 clients at $50/month ($1.8M ARR). Buy for $5-7M (3-4x revenue). Migrate clients to Corner. Those 3,000 clients now pay $1,500-3,000/month for a full AI operations system instead of $50/month for a scheduling tool. Revenue per client increases 30-60x.
  • A CPA practice management tool with 1,500 firms at $200/month ($3.6M ARR). Buy for $10-15M. Migrate to Corner for CPAs. Revenue per firm increases 15x.
  • A restaurant operations tool with 2,000 restaurants at $100/month ($2.4M ARR). Buy for $7-10M. Migrate to Corner for Restaurants.

The Migration Play

Step 1: Acquire. Buy the company. Keep the product running.

Step 2: Announce. "We're joining Corner. Your [Scheduling App] is becoming something much bigger. Same features you love, plus an entire AI team that handles the rest of your operations."

Step 3: Parallel run. Both products run for 6 months. Client can switch at any time. Incentive: 3 months free on Corner for early migrators. Corner's Genesis Agent pre-configures their office using data from the legacy product.

Step 4: Sunset. Legacy product enters maintenance mode. No new features. New signups redirect to Corner. After 12 months, legacy product shuts down. Remaining clients migrated automatically.

Step 5: Retain. Not all clients will upgrade to full Corner pricing. Some will churn. Target: 60-70% retention at higher ARPU. Even if 40% churn, the acquired revenue per client is 15-60x higher. Net revenue increases dramatically.

Revenue Arithmetic

Acquire a 3,000-client app at $50/month ARPU ($1.8M ARR) for $7M.

Post-migration (assuming 60% retention at $2,000 avg ARPU):

  • 1,800 clients x $2,000/month = $3.6M MRR = $43.2M ARR

Investment: $7M. New ARR: $43.2M. Payback: ~2 months of incremental revenue.

This is why acquisition becomes the fastest growth lever after C8. The math is absurd if the migration works.

Why This Is C9

Acquisition requires: (1) enough capital (from C7-C8 revenue or fundraising), (2) a proven migration playbook (Genesis Agent + industry editions), (3) operational capacity to run two products simultaneously during migration. Before C9, AOM doesn't have the infrastructure to absorb another company's client base.

3. International Expansion

Concept

Corner Japan. Corner Germany. Corner Brazil. Corner UK. Corner India. Each market gets localized everything: language (from C6), industry editions (from C7), local franchise operators (from C8), local currency and payment methods, local compliance, and local culture adapted into the game world.

Why International

The US SMB market is $64B (our TAM calculation from the investor pitch). But there are more small businesses outside the US than inside it. The global SMB count exceeds 400 million. If the US is a $64B opportunity, the global opportunity is $500B+.

More importantly: the competitors are US-focused. Nobody is building AI operations for a plumber in Osaka, a CPA in Munich, or a restaurant in Sao Paulo. Corner can own international markets before anyone else shows up.

Market Prioritization

Priority Market Why Entry Method
1 United Kingdom English-speaking. Similar SMB structure. No translation needed. Common law (legal agents transfer). Direct + franchise
2 Canada English + French. Adjacent to US operations. Similar industries. Direct + franchise
3 Australia English-speaking. Strong construction market. Timezone-independent (agents work 24/7). Franchise-first
4 Germany Largest EU economy. Strong Mittelstand (SMB) culture. High AI adoption. Partnership with local IT service provider
5 Japan Massive SMB market (3.8M companies). Technology-forward. Labor shortage makes AI operations compelling. Joint venture with local firm
6 Brazil Largest LatAm economy. 20M+ micro-businesses. Portuguese (already in C6 language pipeline). Franchise-first
7 India 63M+ MSMEs. English-speaking business class. Low cost = lower pricing tier needed. Partnership or franchise
8 Mexico 5.5M SMBs. Spanish (C6 Phase 2). Adjacent to US. Construction boom. Cross-border franchise from Phoenix

What Changes Per Market

Language: Already handled by C6 i18n. But UI translation is not enough. Agent conversation styles need cultural calibration. A Japanese agent is more formal. A Brazilian agent is warmer. A German agent is more precise. Cultural personality mapping per market.

Currency + Payments: Stripe supports 135+ currencies. But some markets need local payment methods: Konbini (Japan), Boleto (Brazil), iDEAL (Netherlands), UPI (India). Corner Pay (C8) needs to support these.

Compliance: GDPR (EU), LGPD (Brazil), APPI (Japan), POPIA (South Africa). Each market has its own data privacy regime. Corner already does per-client data isolation (from C4). The compliance layer adds: data residency (host data in the country), consent management (per-regulation), and data deletion workflows (GDPR right to erasure, etc.).

Industry localization: Construction licenses, tax codes, legal frameworks all differ by country. Industry editions (C7) need country-specific variants. "Corner for Construction (UK)" knows UK building regulations, VAT, and council planning permits. "Corner for CPAs (Germany)" knows German tax law (Steuerberater framework).

Game localization: The isometric office furniture should reflect local culture. A Japanese office has different furniture than a Phoenix office. Tatami mat room themes. German minimalist themes. Brazilian color palettes. Steffen designs cultural room packs.

International Revenue Model

Same pricing, adjusted for market:

  • US/UK/Australia/Canada: $1,500-$10,000/month (current tiers)
  • Germany/Japan: $1,200-$8,000/month (slightly lower, strong currencies)
  • Brazil/Mexico/India: $500-$3,000/month (purchasing power adjusted)
  • Enterprise pricing remains custom everywhere

Franchise model (from C8) is the primary international vehicle.

  • AOM doesn't open offices in Tokyo. A Japanese franchise operator does.
  • AOM provides: platform, updates, training, brand. Franchisee provides: local sales, local support, local market knowledge.
  • Franchise fee adjusted by market: $25k (US/UK), $15k (Brazil), $10k (India)

Why This Is C9

International expansion requires: (1) multi-language product (C6), (2) industry editions that localize (C7), (3) franchise infrastructure that scales (C8), (4) Genesis Agent that can onboard in any language/culture (C9). Before all of these exist, international is premature.

4. IPO Infrastructure

Concept

Corner generates its own SEC filings, board materials, investor updates, and compliance documentation. The product that runs other people's businesses runs its own public company infrastructure. When AOM goes public (or prepares to), the AI team handles the administrative burden.

Why This Matters

Going public costs $5-15M and requires a CFO, controller, general counsel, auditors, investor relations, and a 50-page S-1 that takes 6 months to write. Most of that work is: gathering data, formatting it, ensuring compliance, and communicating clearly. All things AI agents are good at.

Corner's C8 Financial Infrastructure already tracks AOM's money. Corner's Legal agents already handle compliance. Corner's Communications Hub already manages investor relations. C9 connects these into a purpose-built IPO machine.

Components

SOX Compliance (Sarbanes-Oxley):

  • Internal controls over financial reporting (ICFR)
  • Automated quarterly attestation of all financial data
  • Agent-generated control documentation: what control exists, when it was tested, what the results were
  • Audit trail: every financial transaction in Corner Pay traced from source to financial statement
  • Material weakness detection: agents flag anomalies that could indicate control failures

SEC Filing Generation:

  • 10-K (annual report): agents compile financial data, business description updates, risk factors, MD&A
  • 10-Q (quarterly report): same as 10-K but lighter, faster
  • 8-K (material events): agents draft disclosure within hours of a material event
  • Proxy statement: board composition, executive compensation, shareholder proposals
  • S-1 (IPO registration): the big one. Agents draft sections based on years of Corner operational data. Human lawyers review. But the first draft is 90% done by agents.

Board Materials:

  • Monthly board deck: financial performance, product metrics, pipeline, risks
  • Agent-generated with charts from Megaboard data
  • Board portal: secure access for board members to view materials, approve resolutions, sign documents

Investor Relations:

  • Earnings call prep: agents compile talking points, Q&A prep (predict analyst questions from previous calls and market trends)
  • Shareholder communication: annual letter (agent-drafted, Patrik-edited), quarterly updates
  • Investor data room: for due diligence during fundraising or acquisition discussions

Transfer Agent Integration:

  • Cap table management: shares outstanding, options, warrants, convertible notes
  • Dividend distribution (if applicable)
  • Shareholder registry
  • Integration with transfer agent (Carta, Computershare, or corner-native)

The Meta-Play

This is the most recursive thing in the entire spec library. Corner helps SMBs run their operations. One of those SMBs is AOM. AOM is preparing to go public. Corner helps AOM go public. The public company's operations run on Corner. The product IS the infrastructure. Client zero all the way to the Nasdaq.

If AOM can demonstrate that a public company runs on Corner, the enterprise sales pitch writes itself: "We run a public company on this platform. Your 50-person business will be fine."

Why This Is C9

IPO requires: (1) sufficient revenue (~$50M+ ARR for a tech IPO), (2) proven platform (years of operation), (3) regulatory infrastructure (SOX, SEC reporting). This is 4-5 years out at the earliest. But the planning starts early because SOX compliance needs to be baked in, not bolted on.

5. Edge Deployment (Corner Everywhere)

Concept

Corner runs on anything. A construction trailer with a Starlink connection. A fishing vessel in the Pacific. A disaster relief tent. A military FOB. A ranch in Montana with satellite internet. Anywhere there's electricity and a screen, Corner works.

Why Edge

C7 introduced offline mode. C8 introduced Corner Hardware. C9 extends both to the extreme: environments where connectivity is intermittent or absent for days, where power is unreliable, where the "server" is a Raspberry Pi under a table.

This isn't about the typical SMB in Phoenix. This is about the 20% of businesses that operate in environments where traditional cloud software can't reach. Construction sites without fiber. Agricultural operations in rural areas. Mining operations underground. Maritime operations at sea. Field research stations.

Architecture

Corner Edge Device:

  • A ruggedized mini-PC (Intel NUC or equivalent) running Corner locally
  • Full agent capabilities via Claude Code running on-device (when Anthropic supports local models) or via cached context that allows basic operations without the cloud
  • Syncs to Corner Cloud when connectivity returns (same sync protocol as C7 offline mode, but designed for days-long gaps)
  • Battery backup: 4-8 hours on internal battery
  • Environmental: dust-resistant, water-resistant (IP54 minimum), temperature rated -20 to 50 C
  • Cost target: $499-999 (sold as hardware + subscription)

Mesh Networking:

  • Multiple Corner Edge devices on the same job site form a mesh network
  • Agents on different devices can communicate via local mesh (no internet needed)
  • Use case: 3 foremen on a large construction site, each with a Corner Edge, sharing task updates via mesh. When one device gets a satellite signal, it syncs all three to the cloud.

Satellite Integration:

  • Starlink, OneWeb, or Amazon Kuiper as connectivity layer
  • Corner optimizes for high-latency, low-bandwidth satellite connections
  • Agent responses cached locally. Cloud sync happens in batches during connectivity windows.
  • Automatic bandwidth management: critical data (task completions, financial transactions) syncs first. Media (screenshots, video) syncs during off-peak.

Use Cases

Construction (remote sites): A pipeline project 200 miles from the nearest city. 50 workers. No cell signal. The site office has a Starlink dish and three Corner Edge devices. Foremen manage tasks, log safety incidents, and track materials via Corner all day. Twice a day when Starlink gets a clear window, everything syncs to the cloud. The GC in Phoenix sees the updates in their Corner office as if everything happened in real-time.

Agriculture: A 10,000-acre ranch. The ranch manager has a Corner Edge in the truck. Logs cattle counts, tracks equipment maintenance, manages the seasonal crew schedule. Syncs at the farmhouse each evening. The ranch owner in town sees the daily report in their Corner.

Disaster Relief: A humanitarian organization deploys Corner Edge devices to a disaster zone. Aid workers track supplies, manage volunteer schedules, coordinate logistics through Corner. No existing infrastructure needed. The devices connect to each other via mesh and to HQ via satellite.

Maritime: A shipping company puts Corner Edge on vessels. The captain manages crew, cargo, maintenance, and port schedules through Corner. Limited satellite bandwidth syncs critical data. Full sync at port.

Revenue Model

  • Corner Edge device: $499-999 (hardware margin)
  • Edge subscription: $200/month premium on top of standard Corner subscription
  • Mesh networking add-on: $100/month per additional device
  • Satellite integration: partnership with Starlink/etc. (no additional client cost, bundled with Starlink)

Why This Is C9

Edge deployment requires: (1) mature offline mode (C7), (2) hardware manufacturing capability (C8), (3) agent architecture that works with multi-day sync gaps (C9 evolution), (4) mesh networking protocol (new for C9). The market for edge deployment is smaller but dramatically underserved. Nobody is building AI operations for off-grid businesses.

6. Corner for Government v2 (Defense + Intelligence)

Concept

C8 opened FedRAMP for civilian agencies. C9 opens the defense and intelligence community. ITAR, CMMC, JWICS. The contracts are $50M-$500M. The compliance requirements are extreme. The reward is a customer that never churns and pays on time every time.

Why Defense

The US defense budget is $886B (FY2024). The intelligence community budget is $71B. DoD is mandated to adopt AI under multiple executive orders and congressional directives. But the DoD's AI adoption is painfully slow because every product needs to go through a compliance gauntlet that most companies can't survive.

AOM's advantage: by C9, Corner already has FedRAMP Moderate (from C8) and years of operational data in civilian agencies. The jump from FedRAMP Moderate to DoD IL4/IL5 is significant but not impossible.

Compliance Stack

Level What It Is What It Opens
FedRAMP Moderate Civilian agencies (C8) Most federal civilian agencies
FedRAMP High High-impact data Law enforcement, financial regulators
DoD IL4 Controlled Unclassified Info DoD administrative functions
DoD IL5 Higher CUI + National Security Mission-critical DoD systems
DoD IL6 Classified (SECRET) Intelligence, special operations
CMMC Level 3 Cybersecurity Maturity Defense contractors (200k+ companies)

CMMC: The Hidden Goldmine

CMMC (Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification) is required for every company in the defense industrial base. 200,000+ contractors. Most are small businesses (machine shops, component manufacturers, logistics companies). They need CMMC Level 2-3 certification. They don't know how to get it. They can't afford a consultant.

Corner for Defense Contractors: a Corner instance pre-configured with CMMC compliance. The Legal agent tracks compliance status. The Documents agent generates the System Security Plan (SSP). The Operations agent ensures policies are followed. The Audit agent runs self-assessments.

Pricing: $5,000-$10,000/month (premium for compliance). 200,000 potential clients. If 1% adopt: 2,000 clients at $7,500/month = $15M MRR = $180M ARR from defense contractors alone.

Why This Is C9

Defense requires: (1) FedRAMP established (C8), (2) years of compliance track record, (3) clearance-eligible employees (or partner with a cleared firm), (4) the maturity to handle classified data without anyone at AOM seeing it. This is a multi-year investment that starts in C8 and matures in C9.

7. Corner Talent Marketplace

Concept

Humans join the Corner Network alongside businesses. Freelancers, consultants, specialists. Their Corner agent represents them: manages their calendar, handles client communication, tracks their billing, builds their portfolio. When a business on the network needs a specialist, their agent finds one on the talent marketplace.

Why This Exists

The Corner Network (C8) connects businesses. But many tasks still need humans: the plumber who turns the wrench, the CPA who signs the tax return, the designer who creates the concept. Corner can't replace those humans. But Corner CAN connect those humans to businesses more efficiently than LinkedIn, Indeed, or Fiverr.

How It Works

Freelancer/Consultant signs up for Corner:

  • They get a personal Corner office (smaller than a business instance, 2-3 agents)
  • Agents: Calendar (manages availability), Client Comms (handles inquiries), Portfolio (showcases work), Billing (invoicing + payments via Corner Pay)
  • Their profile lives on the Corner Network: skills, availability, rates, reputation score, portfolio samples

Business needs a human:

  • Business's Operations agent: "I need a structural engineer for a 3-day site visit in Phoenix next week."
  • Operations agent searches the talent marketplace
  • Finds 5 structural engineers within 50 miles, available next week, with relevant experience
  • Presents options to the business owner: "Three qualified structural engineers. Top match: Sarah Chen, 4.9 rating, 12 years experience, $175/hour, available Monday-Wednesday."
  • Business owner approves. Sarah's agent and the business's agent coordinate: schedule confirmed, NDA auto-generated (Legal agent), PO created (Finance agent), work order issued

After the engagement:

  • Both parties rate each other
  • Reputation scores update
  • Sarah's agent adds the project to her portfolio automatically
  • Payment processed through Corner Pay (instant, no 30-day invoice waiting)

Revenue Model

  • Freelancer plan: $200-500/month (smaller instance, fewer agents)
  • Marketplace transaction fee: 5% of the engagement value (split: 3% from business, 2% from freelancer)
  • Premium listing: $99/month for featured placement in search results
  • Verified badges: $50/year for background check, credential verification, insurance verification

The Network Effect Squared

C8's Corner Network connects businesses. C9's Talent Marketplace connects businesses to people. Now every participant in the network (business or individual) makes the network more valuable for everyone else. A GC finds subs through the network AND finds inspectors, engineers, and project managers through the talent marketplace. The value proposition becomes: "If you're in business, you're on Corner."

Why This Is C9

Talent marketplace requires: (1) established Corner Network with thousands of businesses (C8 maturity), (2) Corner Pay processing payments reliably (C8), (3) reputation system with meaningful data (years of transactions), (4) Genesis Agent can onboard freelancers (C9 Feature #1).

8. Corner Capital

Concept

AOM becomes a lender. Corner's AI knows more about its clients' businesses than any bank does. Revenue patterns, cash flow, client concentration, seasonal fluctuations, growth trajectory. Corner uses this data to underwrite loans that no bank would make (because banks don't have the data) at rates that are fair (because Corner's underwriting is better).

Why AOM Should Lend

C8 introduced revenue-based financing via partner (Stripe Capital, Clearco). C9 brings it in-house. The reason: the data advantage.

A bank sees: revenue, expenses, credit score, years in business. Four data points.

Corner sees: every task completed, every client interaction, every agent's performance, every email sent, every invoice paid, every pipeline deal, every seasonal pattern, every client's health score, every skill utilization rate, every cash flow forecast. Thousands of data points. Updated in real-time.

Corner can underwrite a loan to a plumber that a bank would reject, because Corner knows the plumber has 3 signed contracts starting next month, his client retention is 95%, and his agents forecasted $180k in Q3 revenue with 87% confidence. The bank doesn't know any of that.

Products

Working Capital Line:

  • $10k-$250k credit line
  • Based on Corner-verified revenue and cash flow data
  • Interest: 8-15% APR (better than merchant cash advances at 30-50%, worse than prime bank loans at 5-7%)
  • Draw and repay through Corner Pay
  • Auto-repayment: percentage of daily Corner Pay revenue goes to repayment
  • Qualification: 6+ months on Corner, minimum revenue threshold, positive agent health scores

Invoice Factoring:

  • Client sends invoice through Corner. Corner advances 85-90% immediately. Client receives remainder (minus 2-3% fee) when invoice is paid.
  • Corner's agents chase the invoice (Collection agent sends reminders, escalation emails, and tracks payment)
  • This is a natural extension of Corner Pay + CRM. Corner already knows the invoice exists, who it's to, and what their payment history looks like.

Equipment Financing:

  • For construction clients who need tools, trucks, or heavy equipment
  • $5k-$100k
  • Corner knows the client's project pipeline and can verify the equipment is needed for a specific job
  • Secured by the equipment
  • Partner with an equipment finance company initially. Corner provides underwriting data, partner provides capital.

Growth Capital:

  • $50k-$500k for businesses expanding (opening second location, hiring, equipment purchase)
  • Based on 12+ months of Corner data showing growth trajectory
  • Revenue share model: Corner takes a percentage of incremental revenue (not a fixed interest rate)
  • This aligns incentives: Corner's agents help the business grow (which grows Corner's revenue share)

Risk Management

The moat in lending is underwriting. Corner's underwriting is better because:

  1. Real-time data. Banks see last quarter's financials. Corner sees this morning's task completion rate.
  2. Predictive intelligence (C7). Corner's models forecast revenue, churn risk, and cash flow. Banks use historical averages.
  3. Early warning system. If a borrower's business is declining (fewer tasks, dropping client health, stalling pipeline), Corner sees it months before a bank would. Corner can adjust: offer a payment holiday, suggest operational changes, or tighten the credit line before the loan goes bad.
  4. Borrower's agents help. Corner isn't just the lender. It's the operational system. If a borrower falls behind, their agents automatically optimize: chase outstanding invoices harder, reduce unnecessary expenses, surface opportunities for new revenue. The AI is working to make the loan perform.

Default handling:

  • If a borrower defaults, Corner's data is the collateral. Corner knows exactly what the business is worth, who its clients are, what its assets are. Recovery is more efficient than traditional lending.
  • Corner does NOT seize the business or its data. That would destroy trust. Instead: workout plans negotiated by AI, restructured payments, temporary credit freezes. Only legal action as a last resort.

Regulatory Requirements

Lending is heavily regulated. AOM needs:

  • State-by-state lending licenses (or partner with a licensed lender)
  • TILA (Truth in Lending Act) compliance: APR disclosure, rate calculations
  • ECOA (Equal Credit Opportunity Act): no discrimination in lending decisions
  • Fair lending audit: regular review of lending patterns for bias
  • Capital reserves: depending on lending volume, may need to maintain reserves

The play (same as C8 financial infrastructure): Partner with a licensed lender initially. AOM provides the underwriting data and borrower acquisition. Partner provides capital and compliance. Revenue share. Once volume justifies it (>$10M outstanding), AOM obtains its own lending license.

Revenue Potential

At 2,000 Corner clients:

  • 20% take a working capital line: 400 lines at $50k avg = $20M outstanding
  • At 12% APR average: $2.4M/year in interest revenue
  • Plus origination fees (1-2%): $200-400k
  • Plus factoring revenue: if 500 clients factor $100k/year in invoices at 2.5% fee = $1.25M/year

Total financial services revenue: $3.5-4M/year from 2,000 clients. This is ON TOP of platform subscription revenue. And it grows with the client's business.

Why This Is C9

Lending requires: (1) years of operational data on borrowers (C7-C8 maturity), (2) financial infrastructure that processes money (C8 Corner Pay), (3) regulatory licenses or partnerships, (4) enough capital or credit facility to lend. This is the highest-stakes feature in the entire spec library. Get it right and it transforms AOM's economics. Get it wrong and it can kill the company.

9. The Self-Replicating System

Concept

Corner's own operations run on Corner. Not as a demo. As the actual production system. AOM's sales agents sell Corner using Corner. AOM's customer success agents onboard clients using Corner. AOM's engineering agents manage the codebase using Corner. AOM's finance agents track revenue using Corner. AOM's compliance agents handle SOX/FedRAMP using Corner.

Why This Is the Final Feature

This is the logical conclusion of everything from C1. Patrik built an AI executive assistant to run his business. That system became Corner. Corner runs other people's businesses. Eventually, Corner runs the business that builds Corner. The system is self-referential. Self-improving. Self-replicating.

What "Self-Replicating" Means

Not literally. Corner doesn't spawn new companies. But it does:

Self-selling: AOM's outreach agents (evolved from Jacob) identify prospects, qualify them, send personalized messages, schedule demos, and follow up. Human salespeople handle high-touch enterprise deals. Everything else is agent-driven. At scale: 10,000 outbound messages/month, 500 demos/month, 50 closes/month. No additional sales headcount.

Self-onboarding: Genesis Agent (Feature #1) handles 95%+ of onboarding. Human intervention only for edge cases, enterprise, and compliance-sensitive clients. The system creates new instances of itself.

Privacy: The Sacred Rule

All of this data is anonymized and aggregated. Always.

Non-negotiable:
